title: SL 4.1 · stratified school sample
prompt:
A school has $1200$ students: $360$ in Year 9, $320$ in Year 10, $280$ in Year 11 and $240$ in Year 12. A sample of $60$ students is to be chosen.

(a) Find the number of students to be chosen from each year group in a stratified sample. [3]

(b) State one advantage of stratified sampling over simple random sampling. [1]

(c) A teacher proposes using the first $60$ students to arrive at school. Explain why this sample is not random. [1]

scheme.text: Every year group is represented in proportion to its size, whereas a simple random sample might by chance under-represent a group.
Early arrivals are a convenience sample: students who arrive early may differ systematically (for example by transport), and not every student has an equal chance of selection.

title: SL 4.1 · systematic sampling bias
prompt:
A factory produces $1500$ items each day. An inspector uses systematic sampling to choose $60$ items.

(a) Find the sampling interval. [2]

(b) The first item chosen is number $17$. Write down the numbers of the next two items chosen and the number of the last item chosen. [2]

(c) A machine develops a fault that damages every $25$th item it makes. Explain why the sample could give a misleading picture of the fault. [2]

(d) State one change to the method that would reduce this risk. [1]

scheme.text: The next two items are $42$ and $67$.
The sampling interval matches the period of the fault, so the sample would contain either all damaged items or none of them.
Either way the defect rate in the sample would be $100\%$ or $0\%$, far from the true rate of $4\%$.
Use a simple random sample, or choose the starting point and interval at random each day so the pattern cannot line up.

title: SL 4.2 · quartiles and outliers
prompt:
Twelve values are: $4,\ 7,\ 8,\ 9,\ 11,\ 12,\ 12,\ 14,\ 15,\ 17,\ 21,\ 35$.

(a) Find the median, the lower quartile and the upper quartile. [3]

(b) Find the interquartile range. [1]

(c) Use the rule that an outlier lies more than $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ above $Q_3$ or below $Q_1$ to decide whether $35$ is an outlier. [2]

scheme.text: The median is the mean of the 6th and 7th values: $\dfrac{12+12}{2}=12$.

title: SL 4.2 · cumulative frequency estimates
prompt:
The times, $x$ minutes, taken by $50$ students to finish a puzzle are summarised below.

| Time $x$ | $0<x\leq10$ | $10<x\leq20$ | $20<x\leq30$ | $30<x\leq40$ | $40<x\leq60$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 4 | 10 | 16 | 12 | 8 |

(a) Write down the cumulative frequencies. [2]

(b) Estimate the median time, using linear interpolation. [3]

(c) Estimate the lower and upper quartiles and the interquartile range. [3]

(d) Assuming times in the last class are spread evenly, estimate how many students took more than $45$ minutes. [1]

scheme.text: Cumulative frequencies for the first three classes: $4$, $14$, $30$.
Cumulative frequencies for the last two classes: $42$, $50$.
The median is the $25$th value, which lies in $20<x\leq30$ (cumulative $14$ to $30$).
$45$ to $60$ is $\dfrac{15}{20}$ of the last class, so about $0.75\times8=6$ students.

title: SL 4.3 · mean sd and transformation
prompt:
A data set is $4,\ 6,\ 7,\ 9,\ 14$.

(a) Find the mean. [1]

(b) Find the standard deviation, correct to three significant figures. [2]

(c) Each value is transformed using $y=3x-2$. Find the mean and standard deviation of the new data. [3]

scheme.text: The mean transforms in the same way as the data: $3(8)-2=22$.
Subtracting $2$ does not change the spread; multiplying by $3$ multiplies the standard deviation by $3$.
New mean $22$ and new standard deviation $3\times3.406=10.2$.

title: SL 4.3 · grouped mean and sd
prompt:
The puzzle times of $50$ students are summarised in this table.

| Time $x$ | $0<x\leq10$ | $10<x\leq20$ | $20<x\leq30$ | $30<x\leq40$ | $40<x\leq60$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 4 | 10 | 16 | 12 | 8 |

(a) Estimate the mean time. [3]

(b) Estimate the standard deviation, correct to three significant figures. [3]

(c) Write down the modal class. [1]

(d) Explain why the answers to (a) and (b) are only estimates. [1]

scheme.text: The individual times are unknown, so each value is replaced by its class midpoint.

title: SL 4.4 · correlation and regression
prompt:
The table shows five pairs of values.

| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 3 | 5 | 6 | 9 | 10 |

You are given $\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)=18$, $\sum(x-\bar x)^2=10$ and $\sum(y-\bar y)^2=33.2$.

(a) Find Pearson's correlation coefficient $r$, to three significant figures. [2]

(b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [3]

(c) Use your equation to estimate $y$ when $x=3.5$. [1]

(d) Interpret the gradient of the line. [1]

scheme.text: Gradient $=\dfrac{\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)}{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}=\dfrac{18}{10}=1.8$, with $\bar x=3$ and $\bar y=6.6$.
The line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$: $y-6.6=1.8(x-3)$.
On average $y$ increases by $1.8$ for each one-unit increase in $x$.

title: SL 4.4 · revision and marks
prompt:
Six students record the number of hours $x$ they revised and their test mark $y$ (out of $100$).

| $x$ | 2 | 4 | 5 | 7 | 8 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 41 | 52 | 58 | 70 | 73 | 88 |

(a) Find Pearson's correlation coefficient and describe the correlation. [2]

(b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$, with coefficients to three significant figures. [3]

(c) Estimate the mark of a student who revises for $6$ hours. [2]

(d) A student suggests using the line to predict the mark after $20$ hours. Explain why this is not appropriate. [2]

scheme.text: The correlation is very strong and positive.
Use the regression facility of the GDC with $x$ as the explanatory variable.
About $64$ marks (this is the mean mark, since $6$ is the mean number of hours).
$x=20$ lies far outside the data range ($2$ to $10$), so this is extrapolation and the linear trend may not continue.
The line would give $144$ marks, which is impossible for a test marked out of $100$.

title: SL 4.5 · venn and expected
prompt:
In a class of $30$ students, $18$ play football ($F$), $12$ play tennis ($T$) and $5$ play both.

(a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen student plays neither sport. [2]

(b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen student plays football only. [2]

(c) In a school of $600$ students with the same proportions, estimate how many play neither sport. [2]

title: SL 4.5 · two dice sevens
prompt:
Two fair six-sided dice are thrown and the scores are added.

(a) Show that the probability that the sum is $7$ equals $\dfrac16$. [2]

(b) The dice are thrown $120$ times. Find the expected number of times the sum is $7$. [1]

(c) The dice are thrown $3$ times. Find the probability that the sum is $7$ at least once. [2]

(d) Find the probability that the sum is at least $10$. [2]

scheme.text: The total number of equally likely outcomes is $36$, and the favourable outcomes are $(1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1)$.
Sum $10$: $3$ outcomes; sum $11$: $2$ outcomes; sum $12$: $1$ outcome.

title: SL 4.6 · independence check
prompt:
Events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A)=0.5$, $P(B)=0.4$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.7$.

(a) Find $P(A\cap B)$. [2]

(b) Show that $A$ and $B$ are independent. [2]

(c) Find $P(A\mid B)$. [1]

(d) Find $P(A'\cap B)$. [1]

scheme.text: This equals $P(A\cap B)$, so the events are independent.

title: SL 4.6 · bag without replacement
prompt:
A bag contains $5$ red and $3$ blue counters. Two counters are drawn one after the other without replacement.

(a) Find the probability that both counters are red. [2]

(b) Find the probability that the counters are different colours. [3]

(c) Find the probability that the second counter is red, given that the first was blue. [1]

(d) Given that the second counter is red, find the probability that the first was also red. [2]

scheme.text: After a blue counter is removed, $5$ of the remaining $7$ are red: $\dfrac57$.

title: SL 4.7 · linear pmf
prompt:
The discrete random variable $X$ has $P(X=x)=kx$ for $x=1,2,3,4$, and zero otherwise.

(a) Find the value of $k$. [2]

(b) Find $E(X)$. [2]

(c) Find $\text{Var}(X)$. [2]

title: SL 4.7 · spinner game fair fee
prompt:
In a fair-ground game a spinner pays out $W$ euros: €10 with probability $0.1$, €3 with probability $0.3$, and nothing with probability $0.6$.

(a) Find the expected payout $E(W)$. [2]

(b) The organiser charges €2 per game. Find the organiser's expected profit per game. [2]

(c) Find the organiser's expected profit over $250$ games. [1]

(d) Find the standard deviation of $W$, to three significant figures. [2]

title: SL 4.8 · binomial four trials
prompt:
The random variable $X$ follows a binomial distribution with $n=4$ and $p=0.5$.

(a) Find $P(X=2)$. [2]

(b) Find $P(X\geq3)$. [2]

(c) Write down $E(X)$ and $\text{Var}(X)$. [2]

title: SL 4.8 · defective items
prompt:
Each item produced by a machine is independently defective with probability $0.05$. A sample of $20$ items is inspected. Let $X$ be the number of defective items.

(a) State two assumptions needed for $X$ to follow a binomial distribution. [2]

(b) Find the probability that at least one item in the sample is defective. [2]

(c) Find the smallest sample size $n$ for which the probability of at least one defective item exceeds $0.9$. [3]

(d) For the sample of $20$, find $P(X\leq2)$. [2]

scheme.text: There is a fixed number of trials ($20$), each with only two outcomes (defective or not), and a constant probability $0.05$ of a defect.
The trials are independent: one item being defective does not affect another.
$P(X\leq2)=P(0)+P(1)+P(2)$, or use the binomial cumulative function with $n=20$, $p=0.05$.

title: SL 4.9 · normal probabilities
prompt:
The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $50$ and standard deviation $8$.

(a) Find $P(X>60)$. [2]

(b) Find $P(40<X<55)$. [3]

scheme.text: Standardise: $z=\dfrac{60-50}{8}=1.25$, or use the normal cumulative function with $\mu=50$, $\sigma=8$.
$P=\Phi(0.625)-\Phi(-1.25)$, or the normal cumulative function between $40$ and $55$.

title: SL 4.9 · plant height percentiles
prompt:
The heights of a plant species, in cm, are normally distributed with mean $50$ and standard deviation $8$.

(a) Find the height $k$ such that $90\%$ of plants are shorter than $k$. [3]

(b) Find the interquartile range of the heights. [3]

(c) In a nursery with $500$ plants, estimate how many are taller than $60$ cm. [2]

title: SL 4.10 · x on y line
prompt:
Five pairs of values $(x,y)$ are $(1,3),\ (2,5),\ (3,6),\ (4,9),\ (5,10)$. You are given $\bar x=3$, $\bar y=6.6$, $\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)=18$ and $\sum(y-\bar y)^2=33.2$.

(a) State which regression line should be used to estimate $x$ from a given $y$. [1]

(b) Find the equation of this regression line, with coefficients to three significant figures. [3]

(c) Estimate $x$ when $y=8$. [2]

scheme.text: The line of $x$ on $y$, since $x$ is being estimated and the line of $y$ on $x$ minimises vertical, not horizontal, distances.
The line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$: $x-3=0.5422(y-6.6)$.

title: SL 4.10 · two regression lines
prompt:
Six pairs of values are $(1,2),\ (2,6),\ (3,3),\ (4,8),\ (5,7),\ (6,10)$, with $\bar x=3.5$, $\bar y=6$ and $r=0.846$.

(a) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2]

(b) Find the equation of the regression line of $x$ on $y$. [2]

(c) Estimate $x$ when $y=9$, using the appropriate line. [1]

(d) A student rearranges the equation in (a) to estimate $x$ when $y=9$ and gets $5.69$. Explain why this differs from your answer to (c). [2]

scheme.text: Use the GDC with $x$ as the explanatory variable (the line passes through $(3.5,6)$).
Swap the roles of the variables in the GDC regression.
The line of $y$ on $x$ minimises vertical distances, so rearranging it does not give the line that minimises horizontal distances.
The two lines coincide only when $|r|=1$; here $r=0.846$, so the lines differ (the product of the gradients is $r^2=0.716$ rather than $1$).

title: SL 4.11 · chi squared two by three
prompt:
A survey of $200$ people records their age group ($A$ or $B$) and their preferred transport (car, bus, bicycle).

| | Car | Bus | Bicycle |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group $A$ | 20 | 30 | 50 |
| Group $B$ | 30 | 30 | 40 |

A $\chi^2$ test for independence is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level.

(a) State the null hypothesis. [1]

(b) Find the expected frequency for Group $A$ and Car, showing your method. [2]

(c) Find the value of the $\chi^2$ statistic. [2]

(d) Write down the number of degrees of freedom. [1]

(e) The $p$-value is $0.211$. State the conclusion, with a reason. [2]

scheme.text: $H_0$: age group and preferred transport are independent.
Expected frequencies are $25,30,45$ in both rows; $\chi^2=\sum\dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}=2\left(\dfrac{25}{25}+0+\dfrac{25}{45}\right)$.
$p=0.211>0.05$, so there is not enough evidence to reject $H_0$.
The data are consistent with age group and transport being independent (this does not prove independence).

title: SL 4.11 · chi squared two by two
prompt:
In a trial, $50$ patients in each of two groups ($X$ and $Y$) were recorded as improved or not improved.

| | Improved | Not improved |
|---|---|---|
| Group $X$ | 30 | 20 |
| Group $Y$ | 18 | 32 |

A $\chi^2$ test for independence is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level.

(a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1]

(b) Show that the expected frequency for Group $X$ and Improved is $24$. [2]

(c) Find the value of the $\chi^2$ statistic. [2]

(d) Write down the number of degrees of freedom. [1]

(e) The $p$-value is $0.0163$. State the conclusion, with a reason. [2]

scheme.text: $H_0$: improvement is independent of group; $H_1$: improvement depends on group.
There is evidence at the $5\%$ level that improvement depends on the group.

title: SL 4.12 · two percentile conditions
prompt:
The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. It is known that $P(X<40)=0.2$ and $P(X>70)=0.1$.

(a) Write down the $z$-values corresponding to $x=40$ and $x=70$. [2]

(b) Write two equations connecting $\mu$ and $\sigma$. [2]

(c) Solve the equations to find $\mu$ and $\sigma$, to three significant figures. [2]

title: SL 4.12 · filling machine
prompt:
A machine fills bottles. The volume $X$ ml is normally distributed with mean $502$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. It is found that $2\%$ of bottles contain less than $495$ ml.

(a) Find the $z$-value for which $P(Z<z)=0.02$. [2]

(b) Find the value of $\sigma$. [2]

(c) Find the probability that a bottle contains more than $510$ ml. [2]

(d) The mean is reset to $\mu$, with $\sigma$ unchanged, so that only $1\%$ of bottles contain less than $495$ ml. Find $\mu$. [2]

scheme.text: Use the inverse normal function with area $0.02$.

title: AHL 4.13 · screening test bayes
prompt:
In a population, $10\%$ of people have a condition $D$. A screening test is positive for $90\%$ of people who have $D$, and positive for $10\%$ of people who do not.

(a) Find $P(D\cap\text{positive})$ and $P(D'\cap\text{positive})$. [2]

(b) Find $P(\text{positive})$. [1]

(c) A person tests positive. Use Bayes' theorem to find the probability that they have $D$. [2]

(d) Comment on your answer to part (c). [1]

scheme.text: Although the test is accurate for each group, only half of those testing positive have the condition, because the condition is relatively rare, so many false positives arise.

title: AHL 4.13 · three factories bayes
prompt:
Three factories $A$, $B$ and $C$ make $50\%$, $30\%$ and $20\%$ of a company's components. The proportions defective are $2\%$, $3\%$ and $6\%$ respectively. A component is chosen at random.

(a) Find the probability that it is defective. [3]

(b) Given that it is defective, find the probability that it came from factory $C$. [2]

(c) Show that the three conditional probabilities of the factories given a defect sum to $1$, and state which factory is most likely to be the source. [2]

scheme.text: Use the law of total probability across the three factories.
$P(A\mid D)=\dfrac{10}{31}$ and $P(B\mid D)=\dfrac9{31}$, so the sum is $\dfrac{10+9+12}{31}=1$.
Factory $C$ is the most likely source, even though it makes the fewest components.

title: AHL 4.14 · quadratic pdf
prompt:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=kx(4-x)$ for $0\leq x\leq4$, and $f(x)=0$ otherwise.

(a) Show that $k=\dfrac{3}{32}$. [3]

(b) Find $E(X)$. [2]

(c) Find $\text{Var}(X)$. [3]

scheme.text: The total area under the pdf is $1$: $\displaystyle\int_0^4kx(4-x)\,dx=1$.
The graph is a parabola symmetric about $x=2$, so the mean is at the line of symmetry.

title: AHL 4.14 · linear pdf median and transform
prompt:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=2x$ for $0\leq x\leq1$, and $f(x)=0$ otherwise.

(a) Find the median of $X$, correct to three significant figures. [3]

(b) Find $E(X)$ and $\text{Var}(X)$. [3]

(c) Find $E(3X-2)$ and $\text{Var}(3X-2)$. [2]

title: SL 5.1 · chord to tangent
prompt:
Let $f(x)=x^2+3x$.

(a) Show that the gradient of the chord joining $(2,f(2))$ and $(2+h,f(2+h))$ is $7+h$ for $h\neq0$. [3]

(b) Hence state the gradient of the tangent at $x=2$, justifying your answer with a limit. [1]

(c) Find the equation of the tangent at $x=2$ in the form $y=mx+c$. [2]

scheme.text: Cancel the common factor $h$ (valid since $h\neq0$) to obtain $7+h$.
As $h\to0$, $7+h\to7$, so the tangent gradient is $7$.

title: SL 5.1 · plant growth rates
prompt:
The height of a seedling is modelled by $h(t)=0.4t^2+2t$ centimetres, where $t$ is the time in days after planting.

(a) Find the average rate of growth between $t=3$ and $t=5$. [2]

(b) Find $h'(t)$ and hence the instantaneous rate of growth when $t=3$. [2]

(c) Find the time at which the instantaneous rate of growth equals the average rate found in part (a). [2]

(d) Explain, using the shape of the graph of $h$, why the instantaneous rate at $t=5$ is greater than the average rate in part (a). [2]

scheme.text: $h''(t)=0.8>0$, so the graph is concave up and the gradient increases with $t$.
$h'(5)=6>5.2$, so the gradient at the right-hand end exceeds the chord gradient.

title: SL 5.2 · cubic intervals
prompt:
Let $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+2$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$ and show that it can be written as $3(x-1)(x-3)$. [2]

(b) Find the intervals on which $f$ is increasing and on which it is decreasing. [2]

(c) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and the local minimum. [2]

scheme.text: Sign diagram: $f'>0$ outside the roots and $f'<0$ between them.
Increasing for $x<1$ and for $x>3$; decreasing for $1<x<3$.

title: SL 5.2 · roots from shape
prompt:
Let $f(x)=2x^3-9x^2-24x+10$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$ and solve $f'(x)=0$. [3]

(b) Find the value of $f$ at each stationary point. [2]

(c) Use the sign of $f'$ to classify each stationary point. [2]

(d) Hence explain why the equation $f(x)=0$ has exactly three real solutions. [2]

scheme.text: Local maximum at $(-1,23)$ and local minimum at $(4,-102)$.
The graph rises from $-\infty$ to the maximum $23>0$, so it crosses the axis once on $x<-1$. It then falls to the minimum $-102<0$, crossing again between $-1$ and $4$.
It then rises to $+\infty$ and crosses a third time for $x>4$. No further crossings are possible since the graph is monotonic between turning points, so there are exactly three solutions.

title: SL 5.3 · negative powers
prompt:
Let $f(x)=3x^2-\dfrac4x+\dfrac5{x^3}$ for $x\neq0$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$. [3]

(b) Find the value of $f'(1)$. [1]

title: SL 5.3 · find the constants
prompt:
The function $f(x)=ax^3+bx$ satisfies $f(1)=5$ and $f'(2)=27$.

(a) Show that $a+b=5$ and $12a+b=27$. [3]

(b) Find the values of $a$ and $b$. [2]

(c) Hence write down $f'(x)$ and show that $f$ has no stationary points. [3]

scheme.text: Since $f'(x)$ is never zero, there are no stationary points.

title: SL 5.4 · tangent and normal
prompt:
The curve $C$ has equation $y=x^2-4x+5$.

(a) Find the coordinates of the point $P$ on $C$ where $x=3$, and the gradient of $C$ at $P$. [2]

(b) Find the equation of the tangent at $P$. [1]

(c) Find the equation of the normal at $P$, giving your answer in the form $ax+by=c$ with integer $a$, $b$, $c$. [2]

title: SL 5.4 · parallel tangents
prompt:
The curve $C$ has equation $y=x^3-3x+1$.

(a) Find the coordinates of the two points on $C$ at which the tangent has gradient $9$. [4]

(b) Find the equation of the tangent at the point with positive $x$-coordinate. [2]

(c) Show that this tangent meets $C$ again where $x^3-12x+16=0$. [2]

(d) Hence find the coordinates of the other point where the tangent meets $C$. [2]

scheme.text: Since $x=2$ is a double root, factorise: $(x-2)^2(x+4)=0$.
The other point has $x=-4$ and $y=9(-4)-15=-51$, so $(-4,-51)$.

title: SL 5.5 · function from gradient
prompt:
A curve has gradient function $f'(x)=6x^2-4x+1$ and passes through the point $(1,4)$.

(a) Integrate $f'(x)$, including a constant of integration. [2]

(b) Find $f(x)$. [2]

(c) Find $f(2)$. [1]

title: SL 5.5 · trapezium overestimate
prompt:
Let $f(x)=x^2+1$. The region $R$ is bounded by the graph of $f$, the $x$-axis, and the lines $x=0$ and $x=3$.

(a) Find the exact area of $R$ by integration. [3]

(b) Use the trapezium rule with three strips of equal width to estimate the area of $R$. [3]

(c) Explain why the trapezium rule gives an overestimate here, and state the size of the overestimate. [2]

scheme.text: $f''(x)=2>0$, so the graph is concave up and each chord lies above the curve.

title: SL 5.6 · product chain rules
prompt:
(a) Differentiate $y=(3x^2+1)^4$. [2]

(b) Let $f(x)=x^2\sin 2x$. Find $f'(x)$. [2]

(c) Find the exact value of $f'\!\left(\dfrac\pi4\right)$. [2]

scheme.text: Chain rule: outer derivative $4(3x^2+1)^3$ times inner derivative $6x$.

title: SL 5.6 · rational extrema
prompt:
Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$.

(a) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{1-x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}$. [3]

(b) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $f$. [3]

(c) Classify each stationary point. [2]

(d) Hence state the range of $f$, giving a reason. [2]

scheme.text: Sign of $f'$: negative for $x<-1$, positive for $-1<x<1$, negative for $x>1$.
$\left(-1,-\tfrac12\right)$ is a local minimum and $\left(1,\tfrac12\right)$ is a local maximum.
As $x\to\pm\infty$, $f(x)\to0$, which lies between the two stationary values, so these are the global extremes.

title: SL 5.7 · concavity and inflection
prompt:
Let $f(x)=x^4-8x^3+18x^2$.

(a) Find $f''(x)$ and show that $f''(x)=12(x-1)(x-3)$. [2]

(b) Find the values of $x$ for which the graph of $f$ is concave up, and those for which it is concave down. [2]

(c) Find the coordinates of the two points of inflection. [2]

scheme.text: Concave up for $x<1$ and $x>3$; concave down for $1<x<3$.

title: SL 5.7 · cubic features
prompt:
Let $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1$.

(a) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $f$. [3]

(b) Use the second derivative to classify each stationary point. [2]

(c) Find the point of inflection, justifying that it is a point of inflection. [2]

(d) Find the gradient of the curve at the point of inflection, and explain why this is the smallest gradient on the curve. [2]

scheme.text: $f(1)=5$ and $f(3)=1$, so the points are $(1,5)$ and $(3,1)$.
$(1,5)$ is a local maximum and $(3,1)$ is a local minimum.
$f''(x)=0$ at $x=2$, and $f''$ changes sign from negative to positive there; $f(2)=3$.
$f'(x)=3x^2-12x+9=3(x-2)^2-3\geq-3$, so the gradient is least at the inflection.

title: SL 5.8 · fence with a wall
prompt:
A farmer has $120$ m of fencing to enclose a rectangular field, using a straight wall as one side. Two sides of length $x$ metres are perpendicular to the wall.

(a) Show that the area of the field is $A=120x-2x^2$. [2]

(b) Find the value of $x$ that maximises the area, and justify that it is a maximum. [3]

(c) Find the maximum area. [1]

scheme.text: The side parallel to the wall is $120-2x$.

title: SL 5.10 · integrate and substitute
prompt:
(a) Find $\displaystyle\int\left(4e^{2x}+\frac3x-\sin3x\right)dx$. [4]

(b) Use the substitution $u=x^2+3$ to find $\displaystyle\int x(x^2+3)^4\,dx$. [3]

scheme.text: For a linear inner function, divide by its coefficient: $\int e^{2x}\,dx=\tfrac12e^{2x}$ and $\int\sin3x\,dx=-\tfrac13\cos3x$.

title: SL 5.10 · curve from gradient
prompt:

scheme.text: Let $u=\cos x$, so $du=-\sin x\,dx$ and the integral becomes $-\int u^2\,du$.

title: SL 5.11 · signed area and area
prompt:

scheme.text: The graph lies below the $x$-axis for $-2<x<2$, so the integral is negative.
Area is the magnitude of the signed integral, since the region is entirely below the axis.

scheme.text: On $(0,3)$ the parabola is above the line, so the integrand is $(4x-x^2)-x=3x-x^2$.

title: AHL 5.12 · smooth join
prompt:
The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x^2+2x$ for $x\leq1$ and $f(x)=ax+b$ for $x>1$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

(a) Given that $f$ is continuous at $x=1$, show that $a+b=3$. [3]

(b) Given also that $f$ is differentiable at $x=1$, find $a$ and $b$. [3]

(c) Show from first principles that $g(x)=|x-2|$ is not differentiable at $x=2$. [3]

scheme.text: Continuity requires these to be equal, so $a+b=3$.
The one-sided limits are $+1$ and $-1$, which differ.
So the limit defining $g'(2)$ does not exist and $g$ is not differentiable at $2$ (the graph has a corner).

title: AHL 5.13 · two lhopital limits
prompt:

(b) $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos2x}{x^2}$ [3]

scheme.text: Direct substitution gives $\dfrac00$, an indeterminate form, so the rule applies.
Direct substitution gives $\dfrac00$; the rule gives $\dfrac{2\sin2x}{2x}$, which is again $\dfrac00$.

title: AHL 5.13 · growth rates and constants
prompt:
(a) Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}x^3e^{-2x}$. [3]

(b) Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^+}x^2\ln x$. [3]

(c) The limit $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x-ax}{x^3}$ exists and is finite. Find the value of $a$ and the value of the limit. [3]

scheme.text: Write as $\dfrac{x^3}{e^{2x}}$, which has the form $\dfrac\infty\infty$.
The denominator tends to infinity, so the limit is $0$.
Write as $\dfrac{\ln x}{x^{-2}}$, of the form $\dfrac{-\infty}{\infty}$.
The form is $\dfrac00$; one application gives $\dfrac{\cos x-a}{3x^2}$, which needs the numerator to tend to $0$ for a finite limit.
Then $\dfrac{\cos x-1}{3x^2}\to\dfrac{-\sin x}{6x}\to-\dfrac{\cos x}{6}$, so the limit is $-\dfrac16$.

title: AHL 5.14 · ladder triangle area
prompt:
A ladder of length $5$ m leans against a vertical wall. Its foot is $x$ m from the wall and its top is $y$ m above the ground. The foot slides away from the wall at $0.3$ m s$^{-1}$. At a certain instant $x=3$.

(a) Find the rate at which the top of the ladder is moving down the wall at this instant. [4]

(b) Let $A$ be the area of the triangle formed by the ladder, the wall and the ground. Find $\dfrac{dA}{dt}$ at this instant. [3]

(c) Find the value of $x$ at which $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=0$, giving your answer to three significant figures. [2]

scheme.text: $x^2+y^2=25$ at all times; differentiate with respect to $t$.
$\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-\dfrac34(0.3)=-0.225$, so the top moves down at $0.225$ m s$^{-1}$.

scheme.text: Take $u=\ln x$ and $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=x$, so $v=\dfrac{x^2}{2}$ and $\int x\ln x\,dx=\dfrac{x^2}{2}\ln x-\int\dfrac x2\,dx$.

title: AHL 5.17 · solids of revolution
prompt:
(a) The region under the curve $y=x^2$ between $x=0$ and $x=1$ is rotated through $2\pi$ about the $x$-axis. Find the exact volume of the solid formed. [3]

(b) The region between $y=x$ and $y=x^2$ is rotated through $2\pi$ about the $x$-axis. Find the exact volume of the solid formed. [3]

scheme.text: The curves meet at $x=0$ and $x=1$ with $y=x$ outer: $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(x^2-x^4\right)dx$.

title: AHL 5.17 · area on the y axis
prompt:
(a) The curve $x=y(4-y)$ and the $y$-axis enclose a region $R$. Find the area of $R$. [4]

(b) The region under $y=e^x$ between $x=0$ and $x=1$ is rotated through $2\pi$ about the $x$-axis. Find the volume of the solid, correct to three significant figures. [3]

(c) Find the area enclosed by $y=\ln x$, the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=0$ and $y=2$. [3]

scheme.text: The curve meets the $y$-axis where $x=0$, that is $y=0$ and $y=4$.
Area $=\displaystyle\int_0^4y(4-y)\,dy=\int_0^4(4y-y^2)\,dy$ (the curve has $x\geq0$ between these values).
Rewrite as $x=e^y$ and integrate with respect to $y$.
